In consulting the biggest opportunity is the first draft of almost everything. Market scans, benchmark tables and early storylines used to take a team two days, and now a decent model can produce a usable version in an hour. That frees senior people to spend time with clients instead of formatting slides. Done well, it also lets smaller firms compete on analysis they could never afford before. The margin story will change a lot.

My worry is that junior consultants stop learning how to build the analysis from scratch. If the model does the first pass, you never develop the instinct for when a number looks wrong. Clients are also starting to ask where the answers came from, and we do not always know. I'd like firms to treat this as a training problem, not only a productivity one, but I'm not sure many will.
The job is fine but I expected faster progression and more technical scope. Nobody has said no to my ideas, but few have gone anywhere yet.

Business schools should stop treating AI as a separate elective. In my job the people who get ahead use these tools as part of normal work, and that is what the school should model. The analytical core was the strongest part. I came in weak on statistics and left able to design a proper experiment and defend the results. The school is compact so you know everyone, and that helped when I started a side project with two classmates which later became a small start-up. Governance has to keep up with the product roadmap, not follow it.

The biggest concern is that planners will accept AI forecasts they do not understand, especially during disruption. A forecast that looks precise can hide wide uncertainty, and then the wrong amount of stock gets ordered. Retail operations also depend on suppliers who may not share clean data, so the models end up trained on partial information. The real risk is overconfidence. Teams need to see the range of outcomes, not one number, before they commit to big orders.

Analysts currently spend hours on document review for car loans. Automated checks could catch missing signatures or inconsistent income data earlier. The real opportunity is faster service, since customers often wait days for a decision. The gains are real, but only if the decisions stay checkable by a person.
